question.preamble: The nurse has reviewed the Nurses' Notes from Day 2 0900 and the Laboratory Results.
question.explanation:
Large cells: without B12, DNA synthesis is impaired while RNA and protein synthesis continue, so precursors grow large but divide fewer times; many die in the marrow (ineffective erythropoiesis), raising LDH and bilirubin. Iron deficiency makes cells small.

Cause: in pernicious anemia, autoimmune gastritis destroys parietal cells, and antibodies block intrinsic factor, so B12 cannot be absorbed in the ileum. It is often associated with other autoimmune diseases such as autoimmune thyroid disease. Metformin and reduced stomach acid (omeprazole) add to poor absorption. Her diet contains B12, and folate is normal.

Priority: she has already fallen twice, has lost position sense and gets up alone at night: injury from falls is the most immediate risk. Her white cell count is only mildly low; glossitis and teaching follow.

question.stem: Which statements by Linda indicate that she understands the teaching? Select all that apply.

options.text: “I will need B12 injections every month for the rest of my life.”
“I'll tell my doctor if the tingling gets worse or my balance changes.”
“Now that my blood count is normal, I can stop the injections.”
“I'll check my feet every day, because I may not feel a cut or blister.”
“Eating liver once a week will keep my B12 up.”
“I can switch to my neighbour's folic acid tablets instead of the injections.”
“The numbness in my feet may take months to improve and might not go away completely.”

question.preamble: The nurse has reviewed the Nurses' Notes from Day 2 1200 and Week 6 1000, the Vital Signs, and the Laboratory Results.
question.explanation:
Response: reticulocytes rose sharply by day 7 (14 to 198 × 10⁹/L), the expected first sign of response, and by week 6 hemoglobin, MCV, white cells and platelets have returned to normal. Neurologic recovery is slower.

Understood: the cause, loss of intrinsic factor, is permanent, so B12 is given for life (Option 1). Nerve recovery takes months and may be incomplete, especially when symptoms were present for a long time (Option 7). Reduced sensation means daily foot checks (Option 4). Worsening neurologic symptoms suggest inadequate treatment (Option 2).

Needs more teaching: stopping injections leads to relapse (Option 3). Folic acid does not treat B12 deficiency and can hide it while nerve damage progresses (Option 6). Dietary B12 cannot be absorbed without intrinsic factor (Option 5).

question.stem: The nurse reviews the Health History and the Physical Assessment. Highlight the findings that are consistent with vitamin B12 deficiency.

highlightTabs.content:
Reason for admission: {The client has fallen twice in the past month, both times at night.|correct} {The client reports feeling tired for several months.|correct}

Neurological symptoms: {The client reports numbness and tingling in both feet for 4 months, “like wearing thick socks.”|correct} {The client feels unsteady when walking in the dark.|correct} The daughter reports {that the client has become forgetful and irritable.|correct}

highlightTabs.content:
Skin: {The skin is pale with a slight yellow tinge.|correct}

Mouth: {The tongue is red, smooth and burning.|correct}

Neurological: {Vibration sense is absent at both great toes, and the client cannot tell whether the toes are moved up or down.|correct} {The Romberg test is positive.|correct} {Pain and temperature sensation in the feet are intact.}

question.explanation:
Anemia: tiredness and pallor; the slight yellow tinge comes from pallor combined with mild jaundice, because abnormal red cell precursors are destroyed in the marrow (ineffective erythropoiesis) and release bilirubin.

Glossitis: a red, smooth, burning tongue, because rapidly dividing cells of the tongue also need B12 to make DNA.

Neurologic findings (unique to B12 deficiency): B12 is needed to maintain myelin. Damage to the dorsal columns of the spinal cord and peripheral nerves causes numbness and tingling in a stocking distribution, loss of vibration and position sense, a positive Romberg test, and an unsteady gait that is worse in the dark, when the client cannot use vision to make up for lost position sense; hence falls at night. Cognitive and mood changes (forgetfulness, irritability, depression) also occur. These can appear before the anemia and become permanent if treatment is delayed.

Not consistent: pain and temperature sensation are usually spared in B12 deficiency. A diet with meat, eggs and dairy supplies B12, so the cause is poor absorption, not intake. No black or bloody stools makes blood loss unlikely.

question.stem: The nurse explains the differences between the two vitamin deficiencies. For each finding, click to specify whether it occurs in vitamin B12 deficiency, folate deficiency, or both.

rows.text: MCV above 100 fL with hypersegmented neutrophils
Loss of vibration and position sense with an unsteady gait
Raised methylmalonic acid
Raised homocysteine
Common in alcohol use disorder and in pregnancy without supplements
Caused by a lack of intrinsic factor

question.explanation:
Both: B12 and folate are both needed to make DNA. Without either, cells keep growing (RNA and protein synthesis continue) but divide poorly, so red cells are large (megaloblastic, MCV above 100 fL) and neutrophils have extra nuclear lobes. Folate needs B12 to be recycled, and both are needed to convert homocysteine to methionine, so homocysteine rises in both.

Vitamin B12 only: B12 is also needed to convert methylmalonyl-CoA, so methylmalonic acid rises only in B12 deficiency; the client's MMA of 1.9 µmol/L with a B12 of 98 pmol/L and normal folate confirm B12 deficiency. Neurologic damage occurs only in B12 deficiency. Intrinsic factor, made by gastric parietal cells, is needed to absorb B12 in the terminal ileum.

Folate only: folate stores last only months, so deficiency develops with poor intake (alcohol use disorder), increased need (pregnancy) or drugs such as methotrexate and phenytoin.

Folic acid alone: it could improve the blood count while the nerve damage progresses, so the nurse advises the client not to take it unless prescribed.

question.stem: Complete the following sentences by choosing from the lists of options.

cloze.text: The client's red cells are large because [[drop0]]. The deficiency is mainly caused by [[drop1]]. The nurse's priority is [[drop2]].

options.text: too little iron is available to make hemoglobin
the spleen releases young red cells early
the cells swell from too much water inside them
DNA synthesis is impaired, so precursor cells grow but divide too few times
blood loss from the stomach
too little folate in the diet
too little vitamin B12 in the diet
antibodies that block intrinsic factor (pernicious anemia)
teaching the client how to give injections
preventing falls caused by loss of position sense
relieving the burning tongue
preventing infection from a low white cell count

question.explanation:
Large cells: without B12, DNA synthesis is impaired while RNA and protein synthesis continue, so precursors grow large but divide fewer times; many die in the marrow (ineffective erythropoiesis), raising LDH and bilirubin. Iron deficiency makes cells small.

Cause: in pernicious anemia, autoimmune gastritis destroys parietal cells, and antibodies block intrinsic factor, so B12 cannot be absorbed in the ileum. It is often associated with other autoimmune diseases such as autoimmune thyroid disease. Metformin and reduced stomach acid (omeprazole) add to poor absorption. The client's diet contains B12, and folate is normal.

Priority: the client has already fallen twice, has lost position sense and gets up alone at night: injury from falls is the most immediate risk. The white cell count is only mildly low; glossitis and teaching follow.

question.stem: For each nursing action, click to specify whether the action is Indicated, Non-Essential, or Contraindicated.

rows.text: Contact the internist to clarify the message before changing the treatment
Give folic acid 5 mg PO daily and hold the cyanocobalamin

question.explanation:

Cyanocobalamin is given IM (or deep subcutaneously); given IV, most of it is lost in the urine before it can be used.

Indicated: an order that conflicts with the diagnosis and the existing plan is clarified with the prescriber before acting. The prescribed IM dose is given. A gait belt and assistance protect the client from falls.

Non-Essential: low B12, high methylmalonic acid and positive intrinsic factor antibodies already confirm the diagnosis; a bone marrow biopsy is not needed.

question.stem: Which statements by the client indicate an understanding of the teaching? Select all that apply.

options.text: “I will need B12 injections every month for the rest of my life.”
“I'll tell my doctor if the tingling gets worse or my balance changes.”
“Now that my blood count is normal, I can stop the injections.”
“I'll check my feet every day, because I may not feel a cut or blister.”
“Eating liver once a week will keep my B12 up.”
“I can switch to my neighbour's folic acid tablets instead of the injections.”
“The numbness in my feet may take months to improve and might not go away completely.”

question.explanation:
Response: reticulocytes rose sharply by day 7 (14 to 198 × 10⁹/L), the expected first sign of response, and by week 6 hemoglobin, MCV, white cells and platelets have returned to normal. Neurologic recovery is slower.

Understood: the cause, loss of intrinsic factor, is permanent, so B12 is given for life (Option 1). Nerve recovery takes months and may be incomplete, especially when symptoms were present for a long time (Option 7). Reduced sensation means daily foot checks (Option 4). Worsening neurologic symptoms suggest inadequate treatment (Option 2).

Needs more teaching: stopping injections leads to relapse (Option 3). Folic acid does not treat B12 deficiency and can hide it while nerve damage progresses (Option 6). Dietary B12 cannot be absorbed without intrinsic factor (Option 5).

question.stem: The nurse reviews the client's history and assessment. Which findings require follow-up? Select all that apply.

options.text: Height of 152 cm
Fine crackles at both lung bases and 2+ ankle edema
Shortness of breath on one flight of stairs and needing two pillows to sleep
Stopped taking her deferasirox 8 months ago
Prominent cheekbones and forehead
Grey-bronze skin and a liver edge 4 cm below the costal margin
Well-healed splenectomy scar
Irregular pulse of 112 beats/min with a “racing and skipping” heart

question.explanation:
Require follow-up: each unit of red cells adds about 200 mg of iron, which the body cannot excrete, and thalassemia also increases iron absorption from the gut. Without chelation (Option 4), iron builds up in the heart, liver and endocrine glands. Iron in heart muscle causes cardiomyopathy: dyspnea on exertion and orthopnea (Option 3), arrhythmias (Option 8), and crackles and edema from heart failure (Option 2). Heart failure is the leading cause of death in thalassemia major. Bronze skin and an enlarged liver reflect iron deposited in skin and liver (hepatic siderosis), which can progress to cirrhosis (Option 6).

Long-standing, not new: marrow expansion to compensate for ineffective erythropoiesis thickens the facial and skull bones in childhood (Option 5), and severe anemia with iron overload of the pituitary and gonads limits growth and puberty (Option 1). Her spleen was removed because enlarged spleens trap and destroy transfused cells (Option 7). These need no urgent action, although her asplenia raises her risk of severe infection.

question.stem: The nurse answers the partner's question. For each statement, click to specify whether it describes beta-thalassemia major, beta-thalassemia trait (minor), or both.

rows.text: Two altered beta-globin genes, one inherited from each parent
Small (microcytic) red blood cells
Usually no symptoms and no treatment needed
Severe anemia by age 1 to 2 years, needing regular transfusions
One altered beta-globin gene; the other is normal
Marrow expansion that thickens the skull and facial bones

question.preamble: The nurse has reviewed the Nurses' Notes from Day 1 1000 and the Laboratory Results.
question.explanation:
Pathogenesis: beta-thalassemia is an inherited defect in making beta-globin chains (gene on chromosome 11). With too few beta chains, excess alpha chains have no partner; they precipitate inside red cell precursors, which die in the marrow (ineffective erythropoiesis) or are destroyed in the spleen (hemolysis). Cells that survive are small and pale with target cells; nucleated red cells appear in the blood. It is common in people of Mediterranean, Middle Eastern, South Asian and Southeast Asian ancestry.

Major: both beta genes are affected (autosomal recessive), so beta-chain production is very low. Severe anemia appears once fetal hemoglobin falls, by age 1 to 2; without transfusion, the marrow expands (thick skull and malar bones, fractures), the spleen enlarges and growth fails. HbF may be up to 90%.

Trait (minor): one gene is affected; there is mild microcytic anemia, usually without symptoms, and no treatment. HbA2 above 3.5% to 4% on electrophoresis is diagnostic; it is often mistaken for iron deficiency.

Both make small cells. If the partner has beta-thalassemia trait, each pregnancy has a 50% chance of a child with thalassemia major (Priya passes one affected gene to every child) and a 50% chance of a child with trait; genetic counselling is offered.

question.stem: Complete the following sentences by choosing from the lists of options.

cloze.text: Priya's red cells are small because [[drop0]]. Her body has accumulated iron mainly because [[drop1]]. The nurse's priority is [[drop2]].

options.text: too few beta-globin chains are made, so cells contain too little hemoglobin
her red cells are destroyed by antibodies
she lacks vitamin B12 to make DNA
she lacks iron to make heme
she eats a diet high in red meat
every transfusion adds iron that the body cannot excrete
her spleen was removed
her kidneys cannot excrete iron
body image concerns about her bones

question.preamble: The nurse has reviewed the Nurses' Notes from Day 1 1530.
question.explanation:
Small cells: hemoglobin is built from globin chains plus heme; with too few beta chains, each cell holds less hemoglobin, so cells are microcytic and hypochromic even though iron is plentiful (ferritin 2,840 µg/L). Giving iron would be harmful.

Iron overload: about 200 mg of iron enters with every unit transfused, and humans have no way to excrete extra iron; ineffective erythropoiesis also increases absorption from the gut. Chelation is started once ferritin exceeds about 1,000 µg/L or after 1 to 2 years of transfusions, and must be taken continuously.

Priority: severe cardiac iron (T2* 7 ms), a falling ejection fraction, crackles, edema and an irregular pulse put her at risk of fatal heart failure and arrhythmias. Liver iron, infection risk and body image matter, but the threat to her circulation comes first.

rows.text: Infuse each unit over 3 to 4 hours and give the furosemide between units
Give oral ferrous sulfate to help her make more hemoglobin
Tell Priya that her urine may turn orange-red during the deferoxamine infusion

question.preamble: The nurse has reviewed the Nurses' Notes from Day 1 1700 and the Orders.
question.explanation:
Indicated: with heart failure, red cells are given slowly with a diuretic between units to prevent fluid overload. Deferoxamine binds iron to form ferrioxamine, excreted in urine and bile, which turns urine orange-red: an expected, harmless effect. Deferiprone can cause agranulocytosis, so the neutrophil count is checked every week and fever or sore throat is reported at once.

Contraindicated: she has iron overload; iron supplements add to the damage. Rapid IV deferoxamine causes flushing, hypotension and shock; it is given by slow continuous infusion.

Non-Essential: her diagnosis is established; electrophoresis does not change before each transfusion. A type and screen (crossmatch) is what each transfusion needs.

question.stem: Which instructions should the nurse include in Priya's discharge teaching? Select all that apply.

options.text: Skip deferiprone on the nights you use the deferoxamine pump
Do not take iron supplements or multivitamins that contain iron
Have your neutrophil count checked every week
Report any change in your hearing or vision
Go to the emergency department for a fever or sore throat, even if you feel well otherwise
You can stop the chelation once your transfusions are spaced further apart
Take a vitamin C 1,000 mg tablet each day to boost your energy
Carry information that you have no spleen and keep your vaccines up to date

question.preamble: The nurse has reviewed the Nurses' Notes from Day 6 1000 and the Vital Signs.
question.explanation:
Include: deferiprone can cause agranulocytosis, and without a spleen she is at risk of overwhelming infection with encapsulated bacteria; fever or sore throat needs urgent assessment and a neutrophil count (Options 3 and 5). Deferoxamine can damage hearing and vision (ototoxicity, retinopathy), so these are checked yearly and changes reported (Option 4). Extra iron worsens overload (Option 2). After splenectomy, pneumococcal, meningococcal and Haemophilus vaccines and medical identification are recommended (Option 8).

Do not include: vitamin C increases iron absorption and, in iron overload, can increase iron toxicity to the heart; it is taken only if the hematologist prescribes it with deferoxamine (Option 7). Iron keeps accumulating as long as transfusions continue, so chelation is lifelong (Option 6). The two chelators are prescribed together for heavy cardiac iron; skipping one reduces iron removal (Option 1).

question.stem: The nurse reviews the client's history and assessment. Which findings require follow-up? Select all that apply.

options.text: Height of 152 cm
Fine crackles at both lung bases and 2+ ankle edema
Shortness of breath on one flight of stairs and needing two pillows to sleep
Stopped taking deferasirox 8 months ago
Prominent cheekbones and forehead
Grey-bronze skin and a liver edge 4 cm below the costal margin
Well-healed splenectomy scar
Irregular pulse of 112 beats/min with a “racing and skipping” heart

question.explanation:
Require follow-up: each unit of red cells adds about 200 mg of iron, which the body cannot excrete, and thalassemia also increases iron absorption from the gut. Without chelation (Option 4), iron builds up in the heart, liver and endocrine glands. Iron in heart muscle causes cardiomyopathy: dyspnea on exertion and orthopnea (Option 3), arrhythmias (Option 8), and crackles and edema from heart failure (Option 2). Heart failure is the leading cause of death in thalassemia major. Bronze skin and an enlarged liver reflect iron deposited in skin and liver (hepatic siderosis), which can progress to cirrhosis (Option 6).

Long-standing, not new: marrow expansion to compensate for ineffective erythropoiesis thickens the facial and skull bones in childhood (Option 5), and severe anemia with iron overload of the pituitary and gonads limits growth and puberty (Option 1). Her spleen was removed because enlarged spleens trap and destroy transfused cells (Option 7). These need no urgent action, although asplenia raises the client's risk of severe infection.

question.stem: The nurse answers the partner's question. For each statement, click to specify whether it describes beta-thalassemia major, beta-thalassemia trait (minor), or both.

rows.text: Two altered beta-globin genes, one inherited from each parent
Small (microcytic) red blood cells
Usually no symptoms and no treatment needed
Severe anemia by age 1 to 2 years, needing regular transfusions
One altered beta-globin gene; the other is normal
Marrow expansion that thickens the skull and facial bones

question.explanation:
Pathogenesis: beta-thalassemia is an inherited defect in making beta-globin chains (gene on chromosome 11). With too few beta chains, excess alpha chains have no partner; they precipitate inside red cell precursors, which die in the marrow (ineffective erythropoiesis) or are destroyed in the spleen (hemolysis). Cells that survive are small and pale with target cells; nucleated red cells appear in the blood. It is common in people of Mediterranean, Middle Eastern, South Asian and Southeast Asian ancestry.

Major: both beta genes are affected (autosomal recessive), so beta-chain production is very low. Severe anemia appears once fetal hemoglobin falls, by age 1 to 2; without transfusion, the marrow expands (thick skull and malar bones, fractures), the spleen enlarges and growth fails. HbF may be up to 90%.

Trait (minor): one gene is affected; there is mild microcytic anemia, usually without symptoms, and no treatment. HbA2 above 3.5% to 4% on electrophoresis is diagnostic; it is often mistaken for iron deficiency.

Both make small cells. If the partner has beta-thalassemia trait, each pregnancy has a 50% chance of a child with thalassemia major (the client passes one affected gene to every child) and a 50% chance of a child with trait; genetic counselling is offered.

question.stem: Complete the following sentences by choosing from the lists of options.

cloze.text: The client's red cells are small because [[drop0]]. The client's body has accumulated iron mainly because [[drop1]]. The nurse's priority is [[drop2]].

options.text: too few beta-globin chains are made, so cells contain too little hemoglobin
the red cells are destroyed by antibodies
the client lacks vitamin B12 to make DNA
the client lacks iron to make heme
the client eats a diet high in red meat
every transfusion adds iron that the body cannot excrete
the spleen was removed
the kidneys cannot excrete iron
body image concerns about the bones
heart failure and arrhythmias from iron in the heart muscle
liver damage from iron deposits
infection after splenectomy

question.explanation:
Small cells: hemoglobin is built from globin chains plus heme; with too few beta chains, each cell holds less hemoglobin, so cells are microcytic and hypochromic even though iron is plentiful (ferritin 2,840 µg/L). Giving iron would be harmful.

Iron overload: about 200 mg of iron enters with every unit transfused, and humans have no way to excrete extra iron; ineffective erythropoiesis also increases absorption from the gut. Chelation is started once ferritin exceeds about 1,000 µg/L or after 1 to 2 years of transfusions, and must be taken continuously.

Priority: severe cardiac iron (T2* 7 ms), a falling ejection fraction, crackles, edema and an irregular pulse put the client at risk of fatal heart failure and arrhythmias. Liver iron, infection risk and body image matter, but the threat to the client's circulation comes first.

question.stem: For each nursing action, click to specify whether the action is Indicated, Non-Essential, or Contraindicated.

rows.text: Infuse each unit over 3 to 4 hours and give the furosemide between units
Give oral ferrous sulfate to help the client make more hemoglobin
Tell the client that the urine may turn orange-red during the deferoxamine infusion
Give the deferoxamine as a rapid IV bolus to remove iron faster
Request a hemoglobin electrophoresis before each transfusion
Check the absolute neutrophil count every week while the client takes deferiprone

question.explanation:
Indicated: with heart failure, red cells are given slowly with a diuretic between units to prevent fluid overload. Deferoxamine binds iron to form ferrioxamine, excreted in urine and bile, which turns urine orange-red: an expected, harmless effect. Deferiprone can cause agranulocytosis, so the neutrophil count is checked every week and fever or sore throat is reported at once.

Contraindicated: the client has iron overload; iron supplements add to the damage. Rapid IV deferoxamine causes flushing, hypotension and shock; it is given by slow continuous infusion.

Non-Essential: the diagnosis is established; electrophoresis does not change before each transfusion. A type and screen (crossmatch) is what each transfusion needs.

question.stem: Which instructions should the nurse include in the client's discharge teaching? Select all that apply.

options.text: Skip deferiprone on the nights you use the deferoxamine pump
Do not take iron supplements or multivitamins that contain iron
Have your neutrophil count checked every week
Report any change in your hearing or vision
Go to the emergency department for a fever or sore throat, even if you feel well otherwise
You can stop the chelation once your transfusions are spaced further apart
Take a vitamin C 1,000 mg tablet each day to boost your energy
Carry information that you have no spleen and keep your vaccines up to date

question.explanation:
Include: deferiprone can cause agranulocytosis, and without a spleen the client is at risk of overwhelming infection with encapsulated bacteria; fever or sore throat needs urgent assessment and a neutrophil count (Options 3 and 5). Deferoxamine can damage hearing and vision (ototoxicity, retinopathy), so these are checked yearly and changes reported (Option 4). Extra iron worsens overload (Option 2). After splenectomy, pneumococcal, meningococcal and Haemophilus vaccines and medical identification are recommended (Option 8).

Do not include: vitamin C increases iron absorption and, in iron overload, can increase iron toxicity to the heart; it is taken only if the hematologist prescribes it with deferoxamine (Option 7). Iron keeps accumulating as long as transfusions continue, so chelation is lifelong (Option 6). The two chelators are prescribed together for heavy cardiac iron; skipping one reduces iron removal (Option 1).

question.explanation:
Improved: ferritin fell from 2,840 to 1,640 µg/L and cardiac T2* rose from 7 to 11 ms (above 10 ms, less severe), showing iron is leaving the heart; BNP has normalized and edema has resolved as heart failure improved. Pre-transfusion hemoglobin is now within the 95 to 105 g/L goal, which also suppresses the marrow expansion that drives extra iron absorption.

Not improved: a neutrophil count of 0.8 × 10⁹/L (below 1.0, severe below 0.5) with a sore throat in a client on deferiprone without a spleen needs urgent action: the nurse notifies the hematologist at once; deferiprone is usually held and the client is assessed for infection.

question.stem: The nurse reviews the client's history and assessment. Which findings require follow-up? Select all that apply.

options.text: Slightly yellow sclerae, normal for him
Vomiting with dry mucous membranes after drinking little while skiing
Lower back and thigh pain rated 9/10, unrelieved by hydromorphone
Painful erection for 3 hours
Spleen not palpable
SpO₂ 97% on room air with clear lungs
Heart rate of 116 beats/min

question.explanation:
Require follow-up: when HbS gives up oxygen it polymerizes; red cells become rigid and sickled, stick to the endothelium and block small vessels, causing ischemic pain in bones, back and joints: a vaso-occlusive crisis, the most common crisis (Option 3). It needs rapid, generous analgesia, usually IV opioids. Priapism is vaso-occlusion in the penis; an erection lasting hours is an emergency that can cause permanent erectile dysfunction, so it is reported at once (Option 4). Dehydration (vomiting, little fluid, cold and altitude) concentrates the blood and triggers sickling (Option 2). Tachycardia reflects pain, dehydration and anemia (Option 7).

Expected: mild jaundice from ongoing hemolysis is usual for him (Option 1). In adults with HbSS the spleen has shrunk from repeated infarctions (functional asplenia), so it is not palpable; this is also why fever is dangerous (Option 5). Normal SpO₂ and clear lungs show no sign of acute chest syndrome yet, but they are rechecked regularly (Option 6).

question.explanation:
Vaso-occlusive crisis (Jordan now): ischemic pain from blocked small vessels, often in bones, back and joints, with a clear chest X-ray. Ongoing hemolysis keeps the reticulocyte count high (about 11%), bilirubin and LDH raised, and hemoglobin near his usual level. The white cell count often rises without infection.

Acute chest syndrome: sickling in the lung vessels (often with infection or fat embolism) causes fever, chest pain, cough, tachypnea, crackles, falling SpO₂ and a new pulmonary infiltrate. It is a leading cause of death and often develops 1 to 3 days into a pain crisis.

Aplastic crisis: parvovirus B19 infects red cell precursors and stops red cell production for about a week. Because sickle cells survive only 10 to 20 days, hemoglobin falls fast, and reticulocytes drop below 1%. It often needs transfusion.

question.preamble: The nurse has reviewed the Nurses' Notes from Day 3 0315 and Day 7 1000 and the Vital Signs.
question.explanation:
Hydroxyurea: it increases fetal hemoglobin (HbF), which does not polymerize and dilutes HbS in each cell, so cells sickle less. It reduces painful crises by about 45% and lowers acute chest syndrome and transfusion needs. It does not change the gene. It suppresses the marrow (neutropenia, thrombocytopenia), so blood counts are checked regularly and the dose adjusted; it should not be used during pregnancy or when planning one.

Emergency signs: fever (risk of sepsis without a functioning spleen), chest pain or dyspnea (acute chest syndrome), priapism, sudden weakness, numbness or speech change (stroke) and pain not controlled at home. Pain that settles at home, his usual mild jaundice and ordinary tiredness do not need emergency care.

Also taught: drink plenty of fluids, avoid cold, altitude and overexertion, take folic acid, keep pneumococcal, meningococcal, influenza and COVID-19 vaccines up to date, and use the incentive spirometer at home when ill.

question.explanation:
Require follow-up: when HbS gives up oxygen it polymerizes; red cells become rigid and sickled, stick to the endothelium and block small vessels, causing ischemic pain in bones, back and joints: a vaso-occlusive crisis, the most common crisis (Option 3). It needs rapid, generous analgesia, usually IV opioids. Priapism is vaso-occlusion in the penis; an erection lasting hours is an emergency that can cause permanent erectile dysfunction, so it is reported at once (Option 4). Dehydration (vomiting, little fluid, cold and altitude) concentrates the blood and triggers sickling (Option 2). Tachycardia reflects pain, dehydration and anemia (Option 7).

Expected: mild jaundice from ongoing hemolysis is usual for this client (Option 1). In adults with HbSS the spleen has shrunk from repeated infarctions (functional asplenia), so it is not palpable; this is also why fever is dangerous (Option 5). Normal SpO₂ and clear lungs show no sign of acute chest syndrome yet, but they are rechecked regularly (Option 6).

question.stem: Complete the diagram by dragging from the choices below to specify what condition the client is most likely experiencing, 2 actions the nurse should take to address that condition, and 2 parameters the nurse should monitor to assess the client's progress.

bowtieActions.text: Give a 2 L IV fluid bolus to flush the lungs
Give the prescribed IV antibiotics without delay
Give meperidine for the chest pain
Give oxygen to keep SpO₂ at 95% or higher
Keep the client flat in bed to reduce oxygen demand

question.explanation:
Condition: fever, chest pain, cough, tachypnea, hypoxemia (89%) and a new infiltrate during a pain crisis define acute chest syndrome. Reticulocytes remain high (not aplastic crisis), and the spleen in an adult with HbSS is atrophied (sequestration is mainly a childhood crisis).

Actions: hypoxemia increases sickling, so oxygen is given; broad-spectrum antibiotics are started at once because infection often triggers or complicates the syndrome. Hematology is called for transfusion (often exchange transfusion to lower the HbS percentage). Meperidine's metabolite can cause seizures; large fluid boluses can cause pulmonary edema and worsen the syndrome; lying flat worsens atelectasis: the client sits upright and uses the incentive spirometer.

Parameters: SpO₂ and respiratory rate show whether lung involvement is improving; hemoglobin, which has fallen from 74 to 63 g/L, guides transfusion.

question.stem: Which interventions should the nurse include in the client's plan of care? Select all that apply.

options.text: Coach incentive spirometry every 2 hours while the client is awake
Assess sedation and respiratory rate every hour while the client uses the PCA
Keep the client sitting upright and assist with walking as tolerated
Increase the IV rate to 250 mL/h to reverse sickling faster
Run the IV fluid at the ordered rate and monitor intake, output and lung sounds
Encourage the client to push the PCA button before every breath to stay pain-free
Check that the red cells for the exchange are leukoreduced and phenotype-matched
Apply cool cloths and a fan to bring the temperature down

question.explanation:
Include: incentive spirometry and sitting upright expand the lung bases and reduce atelectasis, which worsens acute chest syndrome (Options 1 and 3). Opioids are needed for chest and bone pain, but sedation comes before respiratory depression, which would worsen hypoxemia (Option 2). Fluids maintain hydration without overload, which can cause pulmonary edema (Option 5). Clients with sickle cell disease receive many transfusions and often form antibodies against red cell antigens; phenotype-matched, leukoreduced, sickle-negative cells reduce reactions (Option 7).

Do not include: cold causes vasoconstriction and sickling; fever is treated with acetaminophen (Option 8). Only the client presses the PCA button, when needed; pressing it constantly risks oversedation (Option 6). Overhydration can trigger pulmonary edema and worsen acute chest syndrome (Option 4).

question.stem: For each nursing action, click to specify whether the action is Indicated, Non-Essential, or Contraindicated.

rows.text: Stop the PCA infusion
Give a PCA dose so the client does not wake in pain
Stimulate the client, support the airway and give the prescribed naloxone
Remove the oxygen to measure the SpO₂ on room air
Explain to the client's mother why only the client may press the PCA button

question.explanation:
Indicated: a respiratory rate of 8 breaths/min, SpO₂ 86% and increasing sedation mean opioid-induced respiratory depression. The opioid is stopped, the client is roused and the airway supported, and naloxone is given as prescribed (diluted and titrated, so the pain does not return all at once); hypoventilation also increases sickling. PCA by proxy defeats the safety of PCA: a sleeping client cannot press the button, so the family is taught not to.

Contraindicated: more opioid worsens the respiratory depression; removing oxygen from a hypoxemic client is unsafe.

Non-Essential: electrophoresis after the exchange shows the HbS percentage but does nothing for the emergency.

question.stem: Complete the following sentences by choosing from the lists of options.

cloze.text: The client shows an understanding of the teaching when stating that hydroxyurea prevents crises by [[drop0]], that while taking it the client needs [[drop1]], and that the client will go to the emergency department for [[drop2]].

options.text: replacing the sickle cell gene
thinning the blood
strengthening the spleen
raising fetal hemoglobin, which does not sickle
regular blood counts, because it can lower white cells and platelets
a low-iron diet
to stop folic acid
monthly chest X-rays
pain that settles with fluids, rest and the usual tablets
tiredness after a long day
a temperature of 38.5° C or higher, chest pain or shortness of breath, or an erection that will not go away
the usual slight yellowing of the eyes

question.explanation:
Hydroxyurea: it increases fetal hemoglobin (HbF), which does not polymerize and dilutes HbS in each cell, so cells sickle less. It reduces painful crises by about 45% and lowers acute chest syndrome and transfusion needs. It does not change the gene. It suppresses the marrow (neutropenia, thrombocytopenia), so blood counts are checked regularly and the dose adjusted; it should not be used during pregnancy or when planning one.

Emergency signs: fever (risk of sepsis without a functioning spleen), chest pain or dyspnea (acute chest syndrome), priapism, sudden weakness, numbness or speech change (stroke) and pain not controlled at home. Pain that settles at home, the usual mild jaundice and ordinary tiredness do not need emergency care.

Also taught: drink plenty of fluids, avoid cold, altitude and overexertion, take folic acid, keep pneumococcal, meningococcal, influenza and COVID-19 vaccines up to date, and use the incentive spirometer at home when ill.

question.stem: The nurse reviews the Nurses' Notes. Highlight the newborn findings that require follow-up.
question.explanation:
Require follow-up: jaundice that appears in the first 24 hours is pathologic until proven otherwise; physiologic jaundice appears after the first day. Here maternal antibodies are destroying the baby's red cells (hemolysis), releasing unconjugated bilirubin faster than the immature liver can conjugate it. Pallor reflects anemia from hemolysis. The liver and spleen enlarge as they remove damaged cells and make new ones (extramedullary hematopoiesis). Sleepiness, poor feeding and a weak suck can be early signs of bilirubin affecting the brain (acute bilirubin encephalopathy) and need urgent assessment.

Expected newborn findings: bluish hands and feet with a pink trunk (acrocyanosis) in the first day, erythema toxicum (white papules on a red base), congenital dermal melanocytosis over the lower back, and molding of the head after vaginal birth.

History: an Rh-negative mother, an Rh-positive father, no Rho(D) immune globulin after the first birth and an anti-D titer of 1:64 (critical titers are usually 1:8 to 1:32) explain the findings.

Glucose 3.4 mmol/L

columns: Supports Hemolytic Disease of the Newborn

question.preamble: The nurse has reviewed the Nurses' Notes from Day 1 1745 and the Laboratory Results.
question.explanation:
Pathogenesis (answering Grace): during her first delivery, some of the baby's Rh-positive red cells entered her circulation. Her immune system made anti-D antibodies; the first baby was born before that response developed and was not affected. In this pregnancy, her IgG anti-D crossed the placenta, coated the baby's Rh-positive red cells and caused their destruction. A dose of Rho(D) immune globulin within 72 hours of the first birth would most likely have prevented the sensitization.

Supports hemolytic disease: a positive DAT shows maternal antibody on the baby's red cells. Hemoglobin of 118 g/L is low for a newborn (anemia from hemolysis), and 14% reticulocytes show the marrow trying to replace the cells. A total bilirubin of 176 µmol/L at 10 hours is far above expected for that age and, with a known hemolytic cause, is above the phototherapy threshold.

Expected: direct bilirubin is normal: the problem is overproduction of unconjugated bilirubin, not liver or bile duct disease. Glucose is normal.

question.preamble: The nurse has reviewed the Nurses' Notes from Day 1 2300 and the Laboratory Results.
question.explanation:
Rate of rise: 176 to 224 µmol/L in 6 hours is 48 µmol/L, or 8 µmol/L per hour. A rise faster than about 5 µmol/L per hour in the first 24 hours is a red flag for hemolysis.

Meaning: physiologic jaundice begins after 24 hours and rises slowly; breastfeeding jaundice appears in the first week with poor intake (this baby is formula-fed); bile duct obstruction raises conjugated bilirubin, which is normal here.

Priority: unconjugated bilirubin is fat-soluble; when it exceeds the binding capacity of albumin it crosses the blood-brain barrier and deposits in the basal ganglia and brainstem. Early signs are lethargy and poor feeding, progressing to high-pitched cry, hypotonia then hypertonia and arching, seizures and permanent damage (kernicterus: cerebral palsy, hearing loss). Late-preterm birth (37 weeks) and hemolysis increase the risk.

leftContent.intro: The nurse on the postpartum and newborn unit is caring for baby boy Okafor, born at 37 weeks by vaginal delivery 10 hours ago, and his mother, Grace, a 31-year-old G2P2 client.

question.stem: Which interventions should the nurse include in the baby's plan of care? Select all that apply.

options.text: Give glucose water between feeds to flush out the bilirubin
Check the baby's temperature at least every 3 to 4 hours
Protect each bilirubin sample from light
Cover the baby's eyes with eye shields while the lights are on
Apply lotion to the skin to prevent drying under the lights
Feed every 3 hours and record wet diapers and stools
Undress the baby except for a diaper to expose as much skin as possible
Judge the response by how yellow the baby's skin looks

question.preamble: The nurse has reviewed the Nurses' Notes from Day 1 2330 and the Orders.
question.explanation:
Include: blue-green light changes bilirubin in the skin into water-soluble forms excreted in bile and urine without conjugation. Eyes are shielded to protect the retina (Option 4). Maximal skin exposure increases the dose of light (Option 7). Phototherapy can cause overheating or heat loss, so temperature is monitored (Option 2). Feeding promotes stooling (bilirubin leaves in stool) and replaces increased insensible water loss; loose green stools are expected (Option 6). Bilirubin breaks down in light, so samples are shielded to avoid falsely low results (Option 3).

Do not include: lotions and oils can cause burns under the lights (Option 5). Water or dextrose does not lower bilirubin and displaces milk, which is needed for stooling (Option 1). Phototherapy bleaches the skin while serum bilirubin can remain high, so the response is judged by serum bilirubin, not skin color (Option 8).

question.stem: For each nursing action, click to specify whether the action is Indicated, Non-Essential, or Contraindicated while the exchange transfusion is prepared.

rows.text: Continue intensive phototherapy until the exchange transfusion begins
Turn off the phototherapy to observe the baby's skin color
Report the high-pitched cry and difficulty rousing to the neonatologist at once
Place the baby on a cardiorespiratory monitor and keep him warm under a radiant warmer
Give the baby Rho(D) immune globulin
Repeat the direct antiglobulin test before the exchange

question.preamble: The nurse has reviewed the Nurses' Notes from Day 2 0700, the Vital Signs, and the Laboratory Results.
question.explanation:
Indicated: phototherapy continues to lower bilirubin while blood is prepared. A high-pitched cry, poor suck and difficulty rousing are signs of acute bilirubin encephalopathy: urgent exchange transfusion can prevent permanent damage. An exchange transfusion replaces about twice the baby's blood volume in small aliquots, removing bilirubin and antibody-coated cells and correcting anemia; heart rate, breathing, temperature, glucose and calcium are monitored closely.

Contraindicated: stopping phototherapy lets bilirubin rise further; skin color does not reflect serum bilirubin. Rho(D) immune globulin is given to Rh-negative mothers to prevent sensitization; it is never given to an Rh-positive baby, whose red cells it would destroy.

Non-Essential: the DAT is already positive and will not change management.

leftContent.intro: The nurse on the postpartum and newborn unit is caring for baby boy Okafor, born at 37 weeks by vaginal delivery 10 hours ago, and his mother, Grace, a 31-year-old G2P2 client.

question.stem: For each statement Grace makes, click to specify whether it shows that the teaching was understood or that she needs further teaching.

rows.text: “Rho(D) immune globulin won't help me now, because I already have the antibodies.”
“In my next pregnancy, I'll have antibody tests and ultrasounds to check the baby for anemia.”
“Our next baby will be fine, because the problem came from this pregnancy.”
“The baby needs blood tests over the next few weeks, because he can still become anemic.”
“If my baby turns yellow again, we'll just put him in the sunlight at home.”
“My sister is Rh-negative too, so she should ask about the immune globulin in her pregnancy.”

question.preamble: The nurse has reviewed the Nurses' Notes from Day 2 1300 and Day 6 1000 and the Laboratory Results.
question.explanation:
Understood: Rho(D) immune globulin prevents sensitization (given at 28 weeks and within 72 hours after the birth of an Rh-positive baby, and after bleeding, trauma, amniocentesis, miscarriage or ectopic pregnancy); once antibodies exist, it cannot remove them. In later pregnancies the antibody titer is followed and, above the critical titer, middle cerebral artery Doppler ultrasound detects fetal anemia, which can be treated with intrauterine transfusion. Maternal antibodies keep destroying the baby's cells for weeks, so late anemia is watched for. An unsensitized Rh-negative relative benefits from prophylaxis.

Needs further teaching: sensitization is permanent and the disease usually becomes more severe with each Rh-positive pregnancy. Sunlight is not a safe or measurable treatment and can burn or overheat a baby; returning jaundice, poor feeding or sleepiness need prompt assessment.

question.explanation:
Require follow-up: jaundice that appears in the first 24 hours is pathologic until proven otherwise; physiologic jaundice appears after the first day. Here maternal antibodies are destroying the newborn's red cells (hemolysis), releasing unconjugated bilirubin faster than the immature liver can conjugate it. Pallor reflects anemia from hemolysis. The liver and spleen enlarge as they remove damaged cells and make new ones (extramedullary hematopoiesis). Sleepiness, poor feeding and a weak suck can be early signs of bilirubin affecting the brain (acute bilirubin encephalopathy) and need urgent assessment.

Expected newborn findings: bluish hands and feet with a pink trunk (acrocyanosis) in the first day, erythema toxicum (white papules on a red base), congenital dermal melanocytosis over the lower back, and molding of the head after vaginal birth.

History: an Rh-negative mother, an Rh-positive father, no Rho(D) immune globulin after the first birth and an anti-D titer of 1:64 (critical titers are usually 1:8 to 1:32) explain the findings.

question.stem: For each finding, click to specify whether it is expected for a healthy newborn or supports hemolytic disease of the newborn.

columns: Supports Hemolytic Disease of the Newborn

rows.text: Positive direct antiglobulin (Coombs) test
Glucose 3.4 mmol/L
Hemoglobin 118 g/L
Direct (conjugated) bilirubin 8 µmol/L
Reticulocytes 14%
Total bilirubin 176 µmol/L at 10 hours of age

question.explanation:
Pathogenesis (answering the client): during the first delivery, some of the first child's Rh-positive red cells entered the client's circulation. The client's immune system made anti-D antibodies; the first child was born before that response developed and was not affected. In this pregnancy, the client's IgG anti-D crossed the placenta, coated the newborn's Rh-positive red cells and caused their destruction. A dose of Rho(D) immune globulin within 72 hours of the first birth would most likely have prevented the sensitization.

Supports hemolytic disease: a positive DAT shows maternal antibody on the newborn's red cells. Hemoglobin of 118 g/L is low for a newborn (anemia from hemolysis), and 14% reticulocytes show the marrow trying to replace the cells. A total bilirubin of 176 µmol/L at 10 hours is far above expected for that age and, with a known hemolytic cause, is above the phototherapy threshold.

Expected: direct bilirubin is normal: the problem is overproduction of unconjugated bilirubin, not liver or bile duct disease. Glucose is normal.

question.stem: Complete the following sentences by choosing from the lists of options.

cloze.text: The newborn's bilirubin rose by about [[drop0]] over 6 hours, which shows [[drop1]]. The nurse's priority is preventing [[drop2]].

options.text: 20 µmol/L per hour

8 µmol/L per hour
jaundice from breastfeeding

an obstruction of the bile ducts

infection of the umbilical cord

question.explanation:
Rate of rise: 176 to 224 µmol/L in 6 hours is 48 µmol/L, or 8 µmol/L per hour. A rise faster than about 5 µmol/L per hour in the first 24 hours is a red flag for hemolysis.

Meaning: physiologic jaundice begins after 24 hours and rises slowly; breastfeeding jaundice appears in the first week with poor intake (this newborn is formula-fed); bile duct obstruction raises conjugated bilirubin, which is normal here.

Priority: unconjugated bilirubin is fat-soluble; when it exceeds the binding capacity of albumin it crosses the blood-brain barrier and deposits in the basal ganglia and brainstem. Early signs are lethargy and poor feeding, progressing to high-pitched cry, hypotonia then hypertonia and arching, seizures and permanent damage (kernicterus: cerebral palsy, hearing loss). Late-preterm birth (37 weeks) and hemolysis increase the risk.

question.stem: Which interventions should the nurse include in the newborn's plan of care? Select all that apply.

options.text: Give glucose water between feeds to flush out the bilirubin
Check the newborn's temperature at least every 3 to 4 hours
Protect each bilirubin sample from light
Cover the newborn's eyes with eye shields while the lights are on
Apply lotion to the skin to prevent drying under the lights
Feed every 3 hours and record wet diapers and stools
Undress the newborn except for a diaper to expose as much skin as possible
Judge the response by how yellow the newborn's skin looks

question.explanation:
Include: blue-green light changes bilirubin in the skin into water-soluble forms excreted in bile and urine without conjugation. Eyes are shielded to protect the retina (Option 4). Maximal skin exposure increases the dose of light (Option 7). Phototherapy can cause overheating or heat loss, so temperature is monitored (Option 2). Feeding promotes stooling (bilirubin leaves in stool) and replaces increased insensible water loss; loose green stools are expected (Option 6). Bilirubin breaks down in light, so samples are shielded to avoid falsely low results (Option 3).

Do not include: lotions and oils can cause burns under the lights (Option 5). Water or dextrose does not lower bilirubin and displaces milk, which is needed for stooling (Option 1). Phototherapy bleaches the skin while serum bilirubin can remain high, so the response is judged by serum bilirubin, not skin color (Option 8).

question.stem: For each nursing action, click to specify whether the action is Indicated, Non-Essential, or Contraindicated while the exchange transfusion is prepared.

rows.text: Continue intensive phototherapy until the exchange transfusion begins
Turn off the phototherapy to observe the newborn's skin color
Report the high-pitched cry and difficulty rousing to the neonatologist at once
Place the newborn on a cardiorespiratory monitor and maintain warmth under a radiant warmer
Give the newborn Rho(D) immune globulin
Repeat the direct antiglobulin test before the exchange

question.explanation:
Indicated: phototherapy continues to lower bilirubin while blood is prepared. A high-pitched cry, poor suck and difficulty rousing are signs of acute bilirubin encephalopathy: urgent exchange transfusion can prevent permanent damage. An exchange transfusion replaces about twice the newborn's blood volume in small aliquots, removing bilirubin and antibody-coated cells and correcting anemia; heart rate, breathing, temperature, glucose and calcium are monitored closely.

Contraindicated: stopping phototherapy lets bilirubin rise further; skin color does not reflect serum bilirubin. Rho(D) immune globulin is given to Rh-negative mothers to prevent sensitization; it is never given to an Rh-positive newborn, whose red cells it would destroy.

Non-Essential: the DAT is already positive and will not change management.

question.stem: For each statement the client makes, click to specify whether it shows that the teaching was understood or that the client needs further teaching.

rows.text: “Rho(D) immune globulin won't help me now, because I already have the antibodies.”
“In my next pregnancy, I'll have antibody tests and ultrasounds to check the baby for anemia.”
“Our next baby will be fine, because the problem came from this pregnancy.”
“The baby needs blood tests over the next few weeks, because he can still become anemic.”
“If my baby turns yellow again, we'll just put him in the sunlight at home.”
“My sister is Rh-negative too, so she should ask about the immune globulin in her pregnancy.”

question.explanation:
Understood: Rho(D) immune globulin prevents sensitization (given at 28 weeks and within 72 hours after the birth of an Rh-positive newborn, and after bleeding, trauma, amniocentesis, miscarriage or ectopic pregnancy); once antibodies exist, it cannot remove them. In later pregnancies the antibody titer is followed and, above the critical titer, middle cerebral artery Doppler ultrasound detects fetal anemia, which can be treated with intrauterine transfusion. Maternal antibodies keep destroying the newborn's cells for weeks, so late anemia is watched for. An unsensitized Rh-negative relative benefits from prophylaxis.

Needs further teaching: sensitization is permanent and the disease usually becomes more severe with each Rh-positive pregnancy. Sunlight is not a safe or measurable treatment and can burn or overheat a newborn; returning jaundice, poor feeding or sleepiness need prompt assessment.
